query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the high‐temperature BCC phase remains metastable because a relatively weak thermodynamic driving force for transforming to the equilibrium FCC (or ordered) phase (due to the low Al content) is counterbalanced by sluggish atomic diffusion in the multicomponent matrix. Only under thermal conditions that allow sufficient atomic mobility (e.g., slow annealing) does localized Al–induced short-range ordering emerge, lowering the free energy and triggering incipient transformation away from the BCC state.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in a single-phase, high-temperature BCC structure.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatments: one set is rapidly quenched from the high-temperature state to kinetically freeze the BCC structure (baseline), and the other is subjected to slow annealing at a sub-liquidus temperature to enable enhanced atomic mobility.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under inert atmosphere with precise control of annealing temperature (e.g., 700–900 °C) and time. Elemental composition is maintained constant; external contamination and oxidation are minimized.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized segregation or short-range ordering of Al atoms, perhaps at grain boundaries or specific lattice planes, which mediates the free energy reduction required for the transformation.
generation.mechanism: A competition between a modest thermodynamic instability of the BCC phase (which favors a lower-energy phase such as an FCC or ordered structure at lower temperatures) and kinetic hindrance due to sluggish diffusion in the multicomponent alloy. Rapid cooling preserves the high-T BCC state, while extended annealing permits Al redistribution and ordering, initiating the phase transformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Rapidly quenched samples will retain the uniform BCC structure, whereas slowly annealed samples will show the emergence of small FCC or ordered phase precipitates (with associated signatures of Al segregation) in addition to the residual BCC. The fraction of the transformed phase is expected to increase with annealing duration.
generation.baseline: Rapid quenching from the high-temperature BCC state, where minimal atomic diffusion prevents any transformation, preserving the metastable BCC microstructure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold when the thermal processing is in a regime where atomic mobility is limited enough to kinetically trap the high-T state (fast quench) versus when moderate annealing (e.g., 700–900 °C) allows measurable but partial transformation. At temperatures too high or too low relative to this window, either full equilibration or negligible diffusion may occur, setting the boundaries for the observed effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Al re-distribution and the quantitative free energy differences between phases remain uncertain without in situ atomic-scale measurements; the critical annealing times and temperatures for the onset of transformation may require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples from the same batch. Subject one set to rapid quenching from the high-temperature BCC state, and subject the other set to slow annealing at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 800 °C) for a series of time intervals. Use high-resolution X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to measure phase fractions, lattice structures, and detect any localized Al enrichment.
measurements: XRD phase analysis to quantify BCC vs. FCC/ordered phase fractions
TEM imaging to observe microstructural changes and precipitate formation
EDS mapping to detect local Al segregation or short-range order
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If slow annealing does not produce any measurable deviation from the initial BCC structure (no evidence of FCC/ordered phase formation or Al segregation) or if rapid quenching unexpectedly shows similar Al partitioning and phase changes, then the proposed mechanism—that phase stability is governed by the interplay between weak thermodynamic driving forces and sluggish kinetics—will be falsified.

Atomic Interaction-Based Prediction of Phase Formations in High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are of particular interest due to their unique combination of high strength, ductility, and fracture resistance. These properties are largely impacted by the phases and number of phases present in the alloy. Due to the enormous chemical design space, with typically five or six elements present in the alloys in addition to the various processing parameters, the prediction of the number of phases is challenging. While there have been multiple recent reports of phase predictions through data-driven models, an alternate approach is proposed and demonstrated here. In this work, phase prediction is performed using features derived from DFT-calculated pairwise interactions among constituent elements (incorporating bonding and structure) rather than relying solely on traditional elemental descriptors such as electronegativity. By focusing on atomic interaction features, our model provides a novel perspective on the phase stability in HEAs. Ultrastrong ductile and stable high-entropy alloys at small scales

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a class of emerging multi-component alloys, showing superior mechanical properties at elevated temperatures and being technologically interesting. However, they are generally brittle at room temperature, fail by cracking at low compressive strains and suffer from limited formability. Here we report a strategy for the fabrication of refractory HEA thin films and small-sized pillars that consist of strongly textured, columnar and nanometre-sized grains. Such HEA pillars exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths of ∼10 GPa—among the highest reported strengths in micro-/nano-pillar compression and one order of magnitude higher than that of its bulk form—and their ductility is considerably improved (compressive plastic strains over 30%). Additionally, we demonstrate that such HEA films show substantially enhanced stability for high-temperature, long-duration conditions (at 1,100 °C for 3 days). Small-scale HEAs combining these properties represent a new class of materials in small-dimension devices potentially for high-stress and high-temperature application

Predictive multiphase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe ability to predict and understand phases in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is still being debated, and primarily true predictive capabilities derive from the known thermodynamics of materials. The present work demonstrates that prior work using high-throughput first-principles calculations may be further utilized to provide direct insight into the temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution in HEAs, particularly Al-containing HEAs with a strengthening multiphase microstructure. Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases, demonstrating a generalizable approach for exploring potential phase evolution where little experimental data exists.
